mainEntity.name: How old is my Singer sewing machine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Find the serial number, usually stamped on the bed or the slide plate, and enter it above, letters and all. The result is the date Singer allotted that block of numbers, which is close to, but not always the same as, the year the machine was built.

mainEntity.name: Can I find a Singer's value by its serial number?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The serial dates the machine and names its model, which is where any value starts, but condition, the model and what similar machines have actually sold for decide the rest. Many sewing machines have little market value; a record of yours is complete without one.

mainEntity.name: Why does my serial number match more than one block?

acceptedAnswer.text: Singer sometimes allotted overlapping numbers to different machine classes or plants. When that happens the lookup shows every block, and the model of your machine decides which is right.

mainEntity.name: My serial number isn't found. Is something wrong with my machine?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Some prefixes were used by Singer plants whose registers are not in this table (C, and some A, E, T and S serials from Germany and Russia), and a few blocks are missing from the published registers.

Singer serial number lookup

Enter your Singer's serial number to see when Singer allotted it, the model it was allotted to and the factory, from Singer's own registers cross-checked against the ISMACS database.

By Heirloom · Updated November 22, 2026

In short

A Singer serial number is a letter prefix and a number, such as G 7572, stamped on the machine, usually on the bed or the slide plate. Singer allotted numbers in blocks, so a serial gives the date its block was allotted, the machine class and the plant: G 7572 was allotted in 1910. Numbers without a letter are mostly from 1850 to 1899.

Look up a serial number

Enter the letters and the number exactly as stamped. Spaces and dashes don't matter.

Read these before you rely on a date

  • Dates are the dates Singer allotted a block of register numbers, not the date a particular machine was built or sold. Blocks were sometimes used up months later; ISMACS notes, for example, that the last class 115 numbers were allotted in 1935 but machines were still being made in 1936. Present results as 'serial allotted in <year>' or 'made about <year>'.
  • The model is the machine class the block was allotted to. Singer occasionally used numbers on other classes (register footnotes such as G9998117-G9999999 being moved to class 15-30 in 1924 are kept as their own overlapping rows) and collectors have confirmed individual deviations (AG851345 = class 66, Y8642086 = 28K, kept as one-number rows with deviation=true). When several rows match, prefer the narrowest range and report the others.
  • The G prefix was used twice. Cycle 1 runs G1 to G9999999 (1910 to May 1923); cycle 2 restarts at G0000001 and runs to G0999999 (May 1923 to August 1924). Singer writes cycle-2 numbers as seven digits with a leading zero (Singer's own table: 'G-0.566.400', 'G-0.999.999'), while cycle-1 numbers below 1,000,000 are written without leading zeros in the Singer register. Decoder rule: a G number read as seven digits beginning with 0 belongs to cycle 2; any other G number belongs to cycle 1; if a number below 1,000,000 is read and it is unclear whether a leading zero was present, report both. Check: 'G 7572' falls in cycle 1 row G1-G25000, class 27, allotted 1 January 1910 (the Singer register notes this block as 'St. Jean, Quebec'); the cycle-2 alternative G0007572 would be class 15, allotted 22 May 1923.
  • Field 'digits' is the zero-padded width the register tables use for the block: 6 for letter-prefixed numbers below 1,000,000, 7 for larger ones, and 7 for every G cycle-2 row. Machines below 1,000,000 are often stamped without the padding zeros, so a shorter number read from a photo should be left-padded before comparing, except for the G cycle-2 leading-zero rule above. 'digits' is null for numeric-only (pre-1900) rows. Field 'cycle' is 2 only for the second G series and 1 everywhere else.
  • Prefix letters are not unique to one plant. The same letters were used by other Singer factories whose registers are not in this table: A, E, T and some S serials were used at Podolsk (Russia), C at Wittenberge (Germany, from 1908), and two-letter prefixes such as JA-JE (St. Johns, Canada), NA-NC (Anderson, USA), SA-SN (Bonnieres, France), MA (Monza, Italy), PA (Karlsruhe, Germany) and others belong to plants not covered here. Prefixes with no rows here (A, C, E, T, X, and every two-letter prefix outside AA-AT and EA-EX) must not be decoded from this table. The model's own letter suffix (e.g. 15K, 66K) indicates the plant as well and can help confirm a match: 'K' classes come from Kilbowie.
  • Numeric-only serials are not always 19th-century: ISMACS's table from Singer publications lists 'No Prefix' serials used at Bonnieres-sur-Seine, France, from 1970 to 1986. A numeric-only serial on a machine whose style is clearly 20th-century should not be dated from the pre-1900 rows.
  • Pre-1900 (numeric-only) rows come from the ISMACS pre-1900 database, which reconstructs many Elizabethport and New York blocks from sightings of surviving machines. Ranges marked with '~' or '?' in the source are flagged approx=true. Field 'confidence' is 'high' where the row has an exact allotment date and exact range (mostly Glasgow/Kilbowie allotments), 'medium' where only the year is known, and 'low' where the range is approximate or a printed typo had to be corrected. Singer's own year-of-issue table only begins at 611,000 (1871), so rows before 1871 could not be cross-checked (year_check = 'no_table'); for 1850-1870 the year is ISMACS's reconstruction from Singer daybooks and Cooper's figures.
  • Many pre-1889 machines carry two or three numbers. Use the larger Register Number (the first number, usually on the slide plate or bed); the smaller Factory Number is not a serial in this table. Where ISMACS lists the second-number range it is kept as 'second_number_text' for reference only.
  • Overlapping and out-of-sequence blocks are real, not errors: Glasgow/Kilbowie allotments were sometimes made years out of order (e.g. 360500-370499, class 12K, 13 March 1869, overlaps 359501-367913, classes 2K and 3K, 1 December 1871), numbers were re-allotted between factories and classes, and ISMACS records duplicate allotments. A decoder must return every matching row, not the first.
